entries.title: In 1959, the first nuclear-powered merchant ship set sail before the world was ready
entries.content:
By the time naval architecture firm George G. Sharp tasked Jack Heaney with the design of the world’s first nuclear-powered merchant ship, [the Glasgow-born designer](https://oac.cdlib.org/findaid/ark:/13030/c87m0b92) had already broken many styling norms. In the mid-1940s, Heaney transformed routine ocean transport into a festive occasion when he designed the interiors of the [SS *President Wilson* and SS *President Cleveland*](https://www.muralsonthehighseas.com/presidents-cleveland-wilson?lightbox=dataItem-j6o4gj8h) with Hawaiian murals, carved glass panels, and a smoking lounge dressed in playful, exotic wall art. His gift for making the mundane desirable wasn’t confined to ocean liners—New York’s Museum of Modern Art had already put one of [his stackable aluminum chairs on display](https://www.moma.org/momaorg/shared/pdfs/docs/press_archives/1116/releases/MOMA_1946-1947_0099_1947-09-15_47915-36.pdf) in 1947. But nothing in Heaney’s career had prepared him for the commission that reached his drawing board in 1957.

At the time, the shadow of 1945, when the world first witnessed the terrifying power of the atom, loomed large. Following World War II, the United States and Soviet Union were locked in a nuclear arms race, and the public associated splitting atoms with annihilation. Atoms meant war.

To shift that sentiment, President Eisenhower launched his [Atoms for Peace](https://www.eisenhowerlibrary.gov/research/online-documents/atoms-peace) initiative, aimed at demonstrating the civilian benefits of nuclear technology—and the NS *Savannah*, or Nuclear Ship *Savannah*, was to be its flagship. Heaney suddenly had a much more daunting task than usual; he would have to make the feared desirable.

More than half a century since the*Savannah* was decommissioned in 1971, there is no nuclear-powered merchant ship in active commercial service anywhere in the world. Four nations have tried. None succeeded, mostly because the economics were not compelling enough and no one trusted [nuclear ships](https://www.popsci.com/technology/nuclear-powered-cargo-ships-salt/).

In the interim, nuclear reactors have only become smaller and safer. Now, as the true cost of burning oil at sea comes due—commercial shipping produces more than three percent of global greenhouse gas emissions—the economics of nuclear-powered merchant ships may finally be compelling. But the problem Heaney was hired to solve in 1957 still stands in the way, persuading people to trust what they fear.

## The making of a maritime designer

[John “Jack” Heaney](https://oac.cdlib.org/findaid/ark:/13030/c87m0b92) was born in Glasgow in 1904. He grew up during a time when the River Clyde, which runs through the heart of Glasgow, served as the world’s premiere shipbuilding hub, with [nearly 40 shipyards](https://www.clydemarineplan.scot/marine-planning/about-the-clyde-marine-region/) situated on its banks. Heaney studied naval architecture at the University of Glasgow, while taking classes at the Glasgow School of Art and apprenticing at the Fairfield Shipbuilding and Engineering Company.

When Heaney emigrated to New York in 1926, he worked a string of jobs, including a brief stint  as a door-to-door refrigerator salesman, before joining the New York City-based naval architecture firm George G. Sharp, Inc. in 1937. At Sharp, Heaney quickly developed a reputation for having an engineer’s eye and artist’s hand, helping design the interiors of several prominent passenger-cargo ships—a specialized form of merchant ship that is part cruise liner, part cargo vessel—including the [Robin Line](https://www.nytimes.com/1947/08/15/archives/new-vessel-sails-in-african-service-robin-gray-departs-with-12.html), the [Delta Line](https://lastoceanliners.com/line/delta-line-DEL), and the [American President Lines](https://lastoceanliners.com/line/american-president-lines-APL). In 1947, the same year MoMA put his chair on display, Heaney opened his own design firm on West 54th Street in Manhattan. A decade later, the *Savannah* project came across his bow.

Originally tasked with the ship’s exterior design, Heaney eventually assumed responsibility for the ship’s interior styling, too. From stem to stern, it was Heaney’s job to design a nuclear-powered ship that passengers would want to cruise on for pleasure, and that businesses would want to ship merchandise on for commerce.

![black and white image of ship](https://www.popsci.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/first-nuclear-powered-ship.jpg?strip=all&quality=85&amp%3Bw=2048)

The *NS Savannah* was the first nuclear-powered merchant ship. *Image: Contributor / Getty Images /*  Mondadori Portfolio

## Atoms for Peace

Eisenhower had announced the Atoms for Peace initiative four years earlier, in a [December 1953 address](https://www.eisenhowerlibrary.gov/sites/default/files/file/atoms_Binder13.pdf) to the United Nations. The atom, he argued, should be turned from a great destructive force “into a great boon, for the benefit of all mankind.” Under Eisenhower, the U.S. began sharing reactor technology and medical isotopes with allied nations. Atoms for Peace sought to prove that the technology that had obliterated two cities could also light homes, treat [cancer](https://www.popsci.com/category/cancer/), [build harbors](https://www.popsci.com/science/nuclear-bomb-alaska/), and move ships.

The U.S. Navy, meanwhile, saw the advantages of a vessel that could continuously plow the ocean without refueling for months, or even years. The [USS *Nautilus*](https://ussnautilus.org/history-of-uss-nautilus/) was the first atomic-powered vessel, a sub, launching in 1955. By the time Sharp signed Heaney to the *Savannah* project, two more atomic-powered subs were patrolling the world’s oceans (USS *Skate* and USS *Seawolf*). But military vessels primarily keep to military ports, so the public rarely saw them.

Eisenhower needed a civilian showcase that would disassociate atom-splitting from mushroom clouds. That showcase would be Heaney’s NS *Savannah*. As a passenger-cargo ship, the *Savannah* would routinely sail into commercial harbors like Rotterdam, Le Havre, and New York, normalizing nuclear reactors and demonstrating their safety. At least, that was the goal.

## How safe is our A-ship?

In 1959, the same year the *Savannah* launched, *Popular Science* ran a short feature designed to quell readers’ fears: “[How Safe Is Our A-Ship Savannah?](https://books.google.com/books?id=cyYDAAAAMBAJ&lpg=PA108&pg=PA108#v=onepage&q&f=false)” The staff-written story read more like a safety brief than an objective review. While boasting about its efficiency—“on a single loading of A-fuel, the *Savannah* will have a range of 350,000 nautical miles”—the article focused mainly on the “worst possible accidents that might befall the first atomic merchant vessel.” Such caution seemed justified. That same year, Denmark canceled a scheduled visit by the USS*Skate* to Copenhagen, and England agreed to receive visiting [nuclear submarines](https://www.popsci.com/technology/building-nuclear-subs/) only at the remote Isle of Portland, population 12,000, rather than major ports.

*Popular Science*’s initial coverage was not anomalous. “Passengers will receive no more radiation on the *Savannah* than they receive from normal background radiation of the earth in their day-to-day lives,” [*The New York Times*](https://www.nytimes.com/1959/07/26/archives/science-in-review-savannah-will-develop-technology-for-future.html) reassured its readers.

By 1961, however, as the *Savannah* prepared to begin its cargo and passenger service, which commenced in 1962, *Popular Science*’s editors were fully onboard, launching a four-part series that spanned four consecutive issues and more than a dozen pages. The do-it-yourself mini-manual provided detailed instructions for readers to build and sail their own four-foot model of the ship. Four different writers and editors took part in the project: [hull casting one month](https://books.google.com/books?id=8iUDAAAAMBAJ&lpg=PA202&pg=PA202#v=onepage&q&f=false), [superstructure the next](https://books.google.com/books?id=UyYDAAAAMBAJ&lpg=PA150&pg=PA150#v=onepage&q&f=false), then [a working steam turbine](https://books.google.com/books?id=ZyYDAAAAMBAJ&lpg=PA142&pg=PA142#v=onepage&q&f=false), and finally [radio controls](https://books.google.com/books?id=QSYDAAAAMBAJ&lpg=PA185&pg=PA185#v=onepage&q&f=false). Even as *Popular Science* promoted its features, the real *Savannah* was being fitted with Heaney’s final touches.

![Black and white image of a white man assembling a ship model.](https://www.popsci.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/nuclear-ship-model-SS-Svannah.png?strip=all&quality=85)

The January 1961 issue of *Popular Science* shows a model of the *NS Savannah* assembled with screws and dowels. *Image: *[Popular Science, January 1961 issue](https://books.google.ca/books?id=UyYDAAAAMBAJ&lpg=PA150&pg=PA150&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q&f=false)**

## Domesticating the atom

On a conventional ship, fuel is stored low in the hull, in tanks that any port can refill with diesel by hose. But *Savannah*’s single, massive fuel core had to sit in the hull’s center, beneath an opening in the deck, so it could be accessible by overhead crane for refueling. Heaney’s answer to this exterior design problem became the ship’s signature: a streamlined, teardrop-shaped superstructure. *Popular Science*’s writers praised *Savannah*’s sleek, futuristic lines as “graceful as a racing yacht’s,” and called its reactor housing “a well-placed superstructure [that] blends airfoil curves with sharply angled planes for a dazzling effect.”

Below decks, Heaney took the fear problem head on, weaving [Atomic Age motifs into the ship’s interior](https://shiphistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Heaney-Student-Resources.pdf). In the [veranda](https://maritime.org/tour/savannah/veranda.php?pano=nr), the cocktail bar’s backlit wine rack depicted the trilinear chart of the nuclides in blue, red, and yellow glass; the tables ringing the dance floor glowed, their tops lit by “panelescent,” or electrically charged luminescent panels. Even the floor tiles in the [main stairwell](https://maritime.org/tour/savannah/stairwell.php?pano=nr) carried the atomic theme. A separate lounge nearby offered passengers a closed-circuit television view into the reactor containment vessel. Overhead light beamed down through light fixtures adorned with stylized atoms.

In the dining room, sculptor Pierre Bourdelle installed a wall mural titled “Fission.” Nearby, suspended in glass, hung [a small gold model](https://maritime.org/tour/savannah/dining.php?pano=nr) of the NS*Savannah*’s namesake, the 1819 steamship [SS*Savannah*](https://www.todayingeorgiahistory.org/tih-georgia-day/ss-savannah/), the first ship to cross the Atlantic under sail and steam. Heaney hoped such Old World symbolism would make people feel comfortable dining, dancing, and sleeping no more than a dozen yards from a nuclear reactor.

As a design achievement, *Savannah* was a triumph. Her passenger cabins were mostly full from 1962 to 1965, and more than 1.4 million people toured the ship across 46 ports in 13 countries.

![Plats and silverware with atom design.](https://www.popsci.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/NS-Savannah-plates.jpg?strip=all&quality=85&amp%3Bw=2048)

Even the plates and silverware used on the *NS Savannah* had an atomic motif. *Image: Baltimore Sun / Contributor / Getty Images /*  Kim Hairston

## Sunk by economics—and fear

But novelty was never going to be enough to move public sentiment or make *Savannah* pay for itself. The combined ship-and-reactor construction cost ran to [roughly $46 million](https://www.nssavannah.net/ID_31/), three to four times what a [comparable conventional freighter](https://vesselhistory.marad.dot.gov/documents/6670edb8-9f06-4ccb-92e2-dd7b709707ee.pdf) cost at the time, and the ship’s specialized nuclear crew commanded specialized wages. No private insurer would touch a nuclear-powered merchant ship; the U.S. government had to indemnify it instead, [extending $500 million in federal liability coverage](https://vesselhistory.marad.dot.gov/documents/11b92117-75b9-4049-ab01-162ab10da24c.pdf) just to get foreign ports to receive the ship. Every port call required [a small diplomatic mission](https://vesselhistory.marad.dot.gov/documents/11b92117-75b9-4049-ab01-162ab10da24c.pdf) of its own, negotiated weeks in advance, with tugs standing by in case of an accident. Some countries, like Australia, New Zealand, and Japan, never accepted *Savannah*.

By the end of the 1960s, the U.S. Defense Department, [one of merchant shipping’s largest customers](https://vesselhistory.marad.dot.gov/documents/11b92117-75b9-4049-ab01-162ab10da24c.pdf), had concluded that conventional freighters remained the better bet. With no federal appetite left to continue funding a revenue-losing program, *Savannah* was withdrawn from service in late 1971 with no plans to build another.

The timing proved fateful. Two years after *Savannah* was decommissioned, the 1973 oil embargo sent fuel prices soaring; had it still been sailing, the ship’s independence from oil might have tipped the scales for commercial customers, even if the public remained fearful.

## Fear kills future “A-ships”

In 1979, the partial meltdown at [Three Mile Island](https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/doc-collections/fact-sheets/3mile-isle)—eight years after *Savannah*’s own retirement—hardened American public fear of [nuclear power](https://www.popsci.com/science/nuclear-fusion-less-energy/) for more than a generation. The Soviet Union’s [Chernobyl](https://world-nuclear.org/information-library/safety-and-security/safety-of-plants/chernobyl-accident) accident in 1986 and Japan’s [Fukushima](https://world-nuclear.org/information-library/safety-and-security/safety-of-plants/fukushima-daiichi-accident) accident in 2011 reinforced that fear.

Three other nations tried what the U.S. attempted with *Savannah*, and each ran into the same wall. West Germany’s nuclear-powered merchant ship [*Otto Hahn*](https://www.usni.org/magazines/proceedings/1970/july/professional-notes-and-notebook) logged 650,000 nautical miles over a decade before port restrictions and rising costs forced her conversion to diesel in 1979—the same year as Three Mile Island.

Japan’s nuclear-powered [*Mutsu*](https://www.nature.com/articles/310531a0) fared worse. Local fishermen blockaded it in harbor for two years before the ship could even sail, and when its reactor went online in 1974, it leaked. The crew had to [improvise radiation shielding](https://www.nature.com/articles/310531a0) using boiled rice and old socks.

The Soviet Union’s nuclear-powered [*Sevmorput*](https://www.thebarentsobserver.com/nuclear-safety/sevmorput-returns-to-arctic-after-troublesome-year/153256), the last of the four and the only one to operate into the 21st century, has sat idle at a dock in Murmansk since 2024. As of today, not a single nuclear-powered merchant ship plows the seas anywhere on Earth.

## Related 'Century in Motion' Stories

[Before the moon race, explorers wanted to conquer the ocean](https://www.popsci.com/science/underwater-cities-ocean-exploration-history/)

[In 1934, Chrysler bet big on teardrop-shaped cars](https://www.popsci.com/technology/teardrop-car-design/)

[In 1871, cities almost got moving sidewalks. Why are we still waiting?](https://www.popsci.com/technology/moving-sidewalks-history/)

[During WWI, a daredevil pilot helped invent the first ‘drones’](https://www.popsci.com/technology/drones-autopilot-invented-wwi-lawrence-sperry/)

[In 1916, hybrid cars could’ve changed history. But Ford wouldn’t allow it.](https://www.popsci.com/technology/first-hybrid-cars-ford/)

[How the Witch of November doomed the ‘Edmund Fitzgerald’](https://www.popsci.com/science/edmund-fitzgerald-wreck-science/)

[100 years of deep-sea filmmaking and ocean exploration](https://www.popsci.com/technology/underwater-filmmaking-history/)

## Take two?

And yet, military fleets have proven the technology works. The U.S. Navy alone has logged more than [6,200 accident-free reactor-years](https://world-nuclear.org/information-library/non-power-nuclear-applications/transport/nuclear-powered-ships) since 1955. What’s more, reactor designs have advanced significantly since Heaney’s day. [Small modular reactors](https://spectrum.ieee.org/nuclear-powered-cargo-ship), or SMRs, have been engineered to be smaller, safer, and simpler to certify than anything available in 1959. SMRs are now in active development for maritime use, including a Norwegian consortium’s [NuProShip](https://www.vard.com/articles/nuproship-exploring-advanced-nuclear-propulsion-in-shipping) program, and a molten-chloride test reactor that [Core Power](https://www.corepower.energy/) and [TerraPower](https://www.terrapower.com/about/) are building at the Idaho National Laboratory.

The pressure to act has intensified, too. Commercial shipping produces more than three percent of global greenhouse gas emissions—a share that [could climb to 10 percent by 2050](https://www.transportenvironment.org/topics/ships/climate-impact-shipping) if the industry does nothing while the rest of the world decarbonizes. In 2023, the [International Maritime Organization](https://www.imo.org/en/ourwork/environment/pages/2023-imo-strategy-on-reduction-of-ghg-emissions-from-ships.aspx), which governs commercial shipping, committed its member states to a net-zero target by 2050, a goal serious enough that the IMO is now weighing previously unthinkable measures like SMRs.

But none of it matters if nuclear-powered merchant ships remain taboo.

Sixty-five years after Jack Heaney tried to make the atom desirable, the real problem with nuclear reactors was less about the technology and more about public perception. Unfortunately, that perception has kept a viable climate solution off the table for more than half a century, at a cost now measurable in our planet’s atmosphere. As the shipping industry searches for a way to shed its considerable share of global carbon emissions, it is not physics but persuasion that remains unsolved.

*In* [*A Century in Motion*](https://www.popsci.com/century-in-motion/)*, Popular Science revisits fascinating transportation stories from our archives, from hybrid cars to moving sidewalks, and explores how these inventions are re-emerging today in surprising ways.*

The post [In 1959, the first nuclear-powered merchant ship set sail before the world was ready](https://www.popsci.com/technology/nuclear-powered-ship-history/) appeared first on [Popular Science](https://www.popsci.com).

entries.title: You should prepare for your iPhone 18 Pro pre-order right now
entries.content:
If you want an [iPhone 18 Pro](https://appleinsider.com/inside/iphone-18 "iPhone 18") and don't want to wait weeks after they ship, go online now to get your preorder ready. Here's how to do it and what you need to look out for.  
  

![Dark purple iPhone 16 Pro shown from back and front, next to online store interface comparing iPhone 16 Pro and iPhone 16 Pro Max models with pricing and size details](https://media.appleinsider.com/gallery/68951-145307-000-lead-Pre-pre-orders-xl.jpg)  
You can't buy it yet, but you can specify and configure the iPhone 18 Pro model you want - image credit: Apple.

  
Pre-orders for new [iPhones](https://appleinsider.com/inside/iphone "iPhone") always start a few minutes late, depending where you are in the world and whether you're ordering online, or through the app. Then when you get on, certain models [sell out](https://appleinsider.com/articles/24/09/13/iphone-16-pro-max-see-shipping-date-slip-just-minutes-after-preorders-start) in moments.  
  
On the day, all you can do to beat the pre-orders starting late is to keep refreshing both the app and the online store. But there is much more you can do in advance to at least hopefully ensure you get the model, the configuration, and the color, that you want.

entries.content:

![Three silver iPhones with large dual rear cameras stand upright on a table, surrounded by minimalist wooden blocks and a vertical book in soft, neutral lighting.](https://media.appleinsider.com/gallery/68919-145210-IMG_3861-xl.jpg)  
Left to right: Actual iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo

  
The 77 minute event was bookended by the latest iPhone models, a bunch of [Apple Health](https://appleinsider.com/inside/apple-health "Apple Health") updates related to more powerful [Apple Watches](https://appleinsider.com/inside/apple-watch "Apple Watch"), and a smidge on [AirPods 5](https://appleinsider.com/inside/airpods "AirPods"). [Tim Cook](https://appleinsider.com/inside/tim-cook "Tim Cook") made a cameo, Johnny Srouji had a sore throat, and yes, there's a foldable iPhone.  
  
The *AppleInsider* staff comes in many shapes, sizes, and opinions that run the gamut. For every devout staffer hyped about the latest release, there's a skeptic worried about the implications.

entries.title: Over 150 Million Driver's Licenses Have Been Leaked
entries.content:
If you have a driver's license in the U.S or Canada, there's a pretty good chance that your data was recently for sale on the dark web. [A massive hack](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/idscan-confirms-breach-tied-to-153-million-stolen-drivers-licenses/ "open in a new window") at ID verification company IDScan.net compromised records for more than 150 million drivers, resulting in scans of licenses being made available to bad actors. IDScan.net is a Louisiana-based company that provides identity and age verification services for industries ranging from casinos and cannabis dispensaries to hotels and car rentals.

## What happened with the IDScan.net breach?

[According to an incident notice](https://idscan.net/notification-data-security-incident/?7194ef805fa2d04b0f7e8c9521f97343 "open in a new window") on IDScan's website, the company received information "on or around" Sept. 1 that an unauthorized third party was able to gain access to stored customer data, including full names along with driver's license and government-issued ID numbers.

This was around the time that [a major breach was reported](https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/09/fbi-probes-service-selling-153m-drivers-licenses/ "open in a new window") by cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs, who received a tip that driver's license information—including digital scans—was available for sale on the dark web via an identity theft service dubbed Nexus. The platform advertised access to more than 153 million driver's licenses, and Krebs and security researcher Zach Edwards [verified the data](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/02/it-sure-looks-like-hackers-breached-a-major-id-card-verification-service/ "open in a new window") and identified IDScan as the likely source. As [TechCrunch reports](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/10/id-verification-giant-idscan-confirms-data-breach-with-more-than-150-million-drivers-licenses-stolen/ "open in a new window"), the FBI is investigating the breach, and the database has since been taken offline.

## What to do if your drivers license has been compromised

A lost or stolen driver's license creates a high risk of identity theft and fraud, as hackers can use it to open financial accounts and take out loans in your name, commit mail fraud, create a fake ID, and even [develop a synthetic identity](https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/what-is-synthetic-identity-fraud-theft/ "open in a new window") (which combines both real and fake personal data) that could be used to commit a crime. If thieves have access to your physical license or a scan, as in this latest breach, they have a complete set of information, including your birth date and photo, to assume your identity. Fraudsters can also do a lot of damage with just your driver's license number.

If your driver's license information has been compromised in a breach, you should take all the [usual steps against identity theft](https://lifehacker.com/money/seven-things-to-do-if-someone-is-using-your-social-security-number), including pulling your credit reports, monitoring your financial accounts, and setting up fraud alerts. (At this point in the data breach game, your credit should already be frozen unless you are actively applying for a new card or loan, but if you haven't yet, do it immediately.)

Because your driver's license is so valuable to identity thieves, [Experian also recommends](https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/what-should-i-do-if-my-drivers-license-number-is-stolen/ "open in a new window") requesting your driving record, which you can get from your state's department of motor vehicles, and running a background check on yourself. Both can reveal if any fraudulent activities have been carried out in your name—for example, if someone has been pulled over or if there are arrest warrants or criminal charges linked to your identity. You can file a police report for a lost or stolen license and report identity theft if you believe your information is being used fraudulently.

IDScan.net is reportedly alerting individuals affected by this latest breach, and given its scale, you should be on the lookout for a notice. The company is offering credit monitoring and identity protection services to those impacted, and you can call 1-833-516-2980 to enroll.

entries.title: Best time to buy an iPhone in 2026: Buy now or wait?
entries.content:
[Macworld](https://www.macworld.com)

If you’re planning to buy a new iPhone, timing your purchase can save you hundreds of dollars or pounds. There are certain times of year when buying is a bad idea, and others when discounts, trade-in deals and retailer promotions make it much easier to get a bargain.

Apple rarely discounts its newest iPhones directly, but prices often fall after new models launch in September and during major sales events such as Black Friday. In 2026, however, the usual pattern changed: Apple raised prices across the range, with even 2025’s iPhone 17 increasing by £100 and the older iPhone 16 returning to its original price. So if your priority is getting the lowest possible price, right now may not be the best time to buy.

That doesn’t mean you should automatically wait. Whether it makes sense to buy now depends on which iPhone you’re considering. Some models, including the iPhone 17, 17e and Air, are still months away from replacement, while discontinued models such as the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max may become more attractive if retailers clear remaining stock.

In this guide, we explain the best and worst times to buy an iPhone, whether now is a good time to buy each current model, when the best deals are likely to appear, and where to look for them. We’ll also cover whether it’s worth waiting for the next generation and when Apple typically cuts prices on older iPhones.

## The worst time to buy an iPhone

This is generally in the weeks leading up to Apple’s September launch event, or in the early spring, when new models are expected to be announced. Buying just before a refresh means you could miss out on new features or pay full price for a model that’s about to be superseded.

## The best time to buy an iPhone

This depends on where you live:

In the U.K., where most iPhones are sold unlocked and off contract, the biggest savings are typically available during major sales events such as [Amazon Prime Day](https://www.macworld.com/article/2382944/best-iphone-prime-day-deals-october-2024.html) (usually in July and October, and occasionally in March) and [Black Friday](https://www.macworld.com/article/1375699/best-iphone-black-friday-deals-2025.html) in late November. However, worthwhile [iPhone discounts](https://www.macworld.com/article/672801/best-iphone-deals.html) can be found throughout the year if you know where to look.

In the U.S., where people tend to buy iPhones through a carrier, the best time to upgrade is often during Black Friday when networks enhance their offers with larger trade-in values, bill credits, gift cards, or discounted service plans.

## Should you buy a new iPhone now or wait?

![Iphone 17e har en kamera, Iphone 17 Pro har tre. De ligger på ett bord med baksidorna upp.](https://b2c-contenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Iphone17e-17pro.jpg?quality=50&strip=all&w=1200)

Ida Blix

September and the months that follow are a much better time to buy an iPhone than earlier in the summer. July and August are usually poor months to buy a Pro iPhone because Apple’s September launch is so close. The [iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max](https://www.macworld.com/article/2953687/iphone-18-pro-max-2026-release-date-design-specs-price.html) and [iPhone Duo](https://www.macworld.com/article/2629813/iphone-ultra-folding-design-price-specs-release-date.html) have now been unveiled, removing that uncertainty.

If you need a phone now, there’s little reason to wait for another annual refresh, and the iPhone 17, [17e](https://www.macworld.com/article/2881175/iphone-17e-release-date-specs-features-price.html) and Air are also relatively safe purchases because their successors aren’t expected until spring 2027. See: [iPhone 18 and 18e rumors](https://www.macworld.com/article/3188152/iphone-18e-18-2027-release-date-specs-price-cameras.html) and [iPhone Air 2 rumors](https://www.macworld.com/article/3197343/iphone-air-2-release-date-price-features-and-latest-rumors.html).

The iPhone 17 remains the strongest value, with a 120Hz ProMotion display, A19 chip, dual 48MP cameras and 256GB of storage for $799/£799. The 18 Pro and Pro Max make more sense if you want the best cameras, performance or battery life, while the Duo is for buyers specifically interested in Apple’s new folding design.

There is, however, one important reason to wait: [2027 could bring a much bigger iPhone redesign](https://www.macworld.com/article/3136248/iphone-18-pro-20th-anniversary-design-display-battery-camera.html). Apple is rumored to be preparing a [20th-anniversary iPhone](https://www.macworld.com/article/3206297/20th-anniversary-iphone-2027-release-date-rumors-specs-features-price.html) with a near-all-screen curved design, under-display Face ID, possible solid-state buttons, a thinner and more efficient OLED display, larger battery and major camera improvements. That could make 2027 a more significant upgrade year than 2026.

So if your current iPhone is still serving you well, waiting could be worthwhile. Otherwise, buy now if you need a phone, or wait until Amazon’s October sale or Black Friday if price is your main concern.

Wondering which iPhone to buy? Read: [Best iPhone](https://www.macworld.com/article/228816/best-iphone-pro-max-duo-ranked.html) for our ranked recommendations and our [iPhone buying guide](https://www.macworld.com/article/670458/iphone-buying-guide.html) for more in-depth information about cameras, displays, performance, storage, battery life and other key specifications across Apple’s current lineup.

Current guidance about whether it’s a good time to buy an iPhone.

## When does Apple release new iPhones?

Apple has a well-established pattern of releasing new iPhones every year, typically in September. This annual cycle has been remarkably consistent for over a decade, with only rare exceptions.

While September remains the anchor for high-end models, Apple has begun to stagger its iPhone launches. Starting with the iPhone 16e in early 2025 and continuing with the iPhone 17e in spring 2026, Apple now releases more affordable models at separate events earlier in the year – often in March.

The iPhone 18 lineup is expected to take this strategy a step further. In September 2026 Apple launched the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, alongside the foldable iPhone Duo. The standard iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, and iPhone Air 2 are expected to follow in spring 2027.

September launches are usually accompanied by a dedicated Apple keynote, while spring releases are more likely to be announced via a press release although Apple has held [spring events](https://www.macworld.com/article/1484151/apple-spring-event-date-time-how-to-watch-rumors.html). Following the announcement, Apple typically opens pre-orders within a few days, with devices going on sale one to two weeks later. Initial availability can be limited, particularly for the most popular models and storage configurations.

## Should you wait for the iPhone 18?

For most people, there isn’t a strong reason to wait for the iPhone 18. Apple isn’t expected to launch the standard model until spring 2027, so buying an iPhone 17 before the end of 2026 would still give you several months with Apple’s current mainstream model before its replacement arrives.

The iPhone 18 is expected to bring a 2nm A20 chip, potentially 9GB or 12GB of RAM, Apple’s C2 modem and possibly a new 24MP front camera. Extra RAM could prove particularly useful for future Apple Intelligence and Siri features. However, the rear camera system is still expected to consist of two 48MP cameras, while the display may remain broadly similar to the iPhone 17’s 6.3-inch ProMotion panel.

There is also some uncertainty over exactly what the iPhone 18 lineup will look like. A September 2026 rumour suggested Apple could effectively merge the standard iPhone and iPhone Air into a single model, rather than continuing them as two separate devices. If that happens, the iPhone 18 could adopt some of the Air’s thinner, lighter design while retaining the broader appeal of the standard iPhone. For now, though, that remains speculative.

Price is another consideration. With the arrival of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, [Apple increased iPhone prices](https://www.macworld.com/article/3229342/iphone-price-increases.html) across the range, so the iPhone 17 now costs $899, $100 more than at launch. When the iPhone 18 arrives, it is likely to inherit that $899 price point, while the iPhone 17 could drop back to around $799 at which you may regret buying it at the higher price.

**Wait if** you want the newer A20 chip, potentially more RAM, an improved front camera, or are intrigued by the possibility of a thinner redesigned standard model.

**Don’t wait if** you simply want ProMotion, dual 48MP cameras, excellent battery life and 256GB of storage as standard – the iPhone 17 already delivers all of that.

## Should you buy a current or older iPhone?

Thinking of buying the current iPhone rather than waiting for a new model? Read on for expert guidance.

If you don’t need a new phone immediately, though, it may be worth waiting for a deal. The best discounts are likely during **Amazon’s October sales and Black Friday on November 27**, when retailers and mobile networks often offer lower prices, trade-in bonuses or contract incentives.

Waiting until spring 2027 only makes sense if you specifically want the expected [iPhone 18](https://www.macworld.com/article/3188152/iphone-18e-18-2027-release-date-specs-price-cameras.html) upgrades, such as the A20 chip, more RAM or an improved front camera. ## FAQ

1.

### When is the best carrier upgrade timing?

Apple typically announces new iPhone models in September. Carriers often roll out their most aggressive trade-in offers and promotional deals around this time to entice customers to upgrade.

**New releases**: Waiting for the September (or spring) launch window is generally a good strategy if you want the latest model at a potentially better subsidized price.

**Check your contract cycle:** Many carrier contracts today last 24 to 36 months. If you’re nearing the end of your contract, you’re in a strong position to negotiate or take advantage of upgrade offers. However, upgrading mid-contract may involve paying off the remaining balance, so it’s worth checking your specific terms.

**Consider Apple’s upgrade plans:** Apple has replaced its old iPhone Upgrade Program with newer financing and leasing options. In the U.S., Apple Upgrade lets you lease an iPhone through Klarna and upgrade, buy or return it at the end of the term. In the U.K., Apple’s Flexible Finance Account offers eligible iPhones on monthly payment plans with the option to upgrade after a set number of payments. Terms and monthly costs vary by model.

2.

### When does Apple update the iPhone?

Apple follows a well-established annual rhythm for its iPhone updates, with the primary event taking place in September each year.

Apple typically unveils its new iPhone lineup at a dedicated [Apple Event in September](https://www.macworld.com/article/831417/apple-september-iphone-event-date-time.html). Pre-orders usually open on the Friday following the announcement, with devices shipping and arriving in stores a week later.

Apple also occasionally introduces new iPhones outside the September window and in the past it has held a [Spring Apple Event](https://www.macworld.com/article/1484151/apple-spring-event-date-time-how-to-watch-rumors.html) at which more affordable iPhones have launched. The iPhone 17e, for example, arrived in March 2026, and the iPhone 16e launched in February 2025.

Compatible iPhone models also get a yearly operating system software update with new features than can make your old iPhone feel new again. The major iOS updates follow the September schedule.

Read our guide to [the next Apple event](https://www.macworld.com/article/672537/when-is-apples-next-event.html) to find out if an Apple event is imminent.

3.

### When do iPhone prices drop and by how much?

Based on past experience, Apple is very unlikely to reduce the price of a new iPhone during its first year on sale.

However, when Apple introduces a new generation of iPhones, it usually cuts the price of the previous year’s models. That means September has traditionally been the point when older iPhones become cheaper.

Apple also tends to keep launch prices broadly similar from one generation to the next, at least in the U.S., although exchange rates and other regional factors can affect pricing elsewhere.

In 2024, for example, Apple reduced the price of the iPhone 15 and iPhone 15 Plus by $100/£100 when the iPhone 16 and 16 Plus arrived. The iPhone 16 also fell in price following the launch of the iPhone 17 in 2025. However, because the iPhone 17 doubled the base storage to 256GB, the older iPhone 16 looked less attractive even at $100/£100 less.

In 2026, the pattern changed. Apple actually [raised iPhone prices](https://www.macworld.com/article/3229342/iphone-price-increases.html), blaming higher memory costs. Even the year-old iPhone 17 and two-year-old iPhone 16 increased by $100, showing that older iPhones don’t always become cheaper when a new generation arrives.

4.

### Is it better to buy from Apple or a carrier?

In the U.S., buying from Apple is usually the better option if you value flexibility. If you pay in full or use Apple’s own financing, the iPhone is unlocked, so you can switch carriers or use another eSIM when traveling. Apple also accepts trade-ins and, importantly, many AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon promotions are available when buying through Apple.

However, an iPhone bought from Apple but financed through an AT&T, T-Mobile or Verizon device-payment plan is locked to that carrier until it has been paid off. An iPhone bought outright from Apple isn’t.

The main reason to buy directly from AT&T, T-Mobile or Verizon is to take advantage of a particularly good promotion. U.S. carriers frequently advertise large trade-in credits or “free” iPhones, especially when you add a line or switch networks. The catch is that the discount is usually provided as monthly bill credits over 24 or 36 months, so if you leave early you can lose the remaining credits.

In the U.K., Apple sells iPhones unlocked and SIM-free, allowing you to shop separately for a SIM-only plan from EE, Vodafone, O2, Three or an MVNO. This makes it easier to switch networks and can work out cheaper over the life of the phone than bundling the handset and airtime into a single contract.

Apple isn’t necessarily the cheapest place to buy, however. Amazon U.K. and other retailers frequently discount SIM-free iPhones, and there can be substantial savings during sales events such as Black Friday.

Networks can also offer compelling promotions, including enhanced trade-in values, discounted airtime, generous data allowances or lower monthly payments. But make sure you compare the total cost of the contract, rather than focusing on the headline monthly price.

5.

### When are the best iPhone deals?

The earliest you could expect to get a discount on the newest iPhones is around Black Friday at the end of November, so you might be planning to hold out until then. However, the deals we tend to see, if any, are usually for older handsets. See our round-up of [Best Black Friday iPhone deals](https://www.macworld.com/article/1375699/best-iphone-cyber-monday-deals-2024.html) for more.

Nor should you expect to get a discount in an [Apple Black Friday sale](https://www.macworld.com/article/672787/apple-black-friday.html). Apple’s Black Friday sale usually only takes the form of vouchers with select product purchases, rather than a discount, and it is unlikely that the newest iPhone would qualify as in previous year’s new iPhones haven’t been included.

Note that while shopping events like Black Friday gets all the attention, that’s not the only time you can get discounts on Apple products: we see discounts all the time. Another event where we see good iPhone deals is Prime Day, which happens in June or July and October every year. So take a look at the [iPhone deals for Amazon Prime Day](https://www.macworld.com/article/2382944/best-iphone-prime-day-deals-2025-jul-11.html) sale to see what you might be able to save.

In our experience, we don’t tend to see discounts on the newest handset until the spring – and these are always from third-party resellers, never from Apple. In fact, we don’t tend to see the iPhone discounted in the U.S. very often, most of the discounts we see are in the U.K. where unlocked iPhones are often sold off-contract at a good discount.

6.

### Is it worth buying a refurbished iPhone?

Yes, buying a refurbished iPhone is absolutely worth it for most people, especially if you want to save money without sacrificing quality.

Buying refurbished is a great way to “pick up a bargain” while still getting a premium device. You can typically save 15% to 30% compared to buying new, and sometimes much more on older models.

A common misconception is that refurbished is the same as buying a used phone from a stranger, though. It’s not. A used phone is sold “as-is,” with no guarantee it will work properly. A refurbished phone has been professionally inspected, tested, and repaired if needed, and it comes with a warranty.

If you want the highest quality, Apple’s own [refurbished store](https://apple.sjv.io/c/321564/435031/7613?subid1=rss&u=https://www.apple.com/shop/refurbished/iphone) is the gold standard.

## Conclusion: When is the best time to buy a new iPhone?

The worst time to buy is usually between July or August, mainly because with new iPhones on the horizon the price of the older handsets are likely to drop very soon.

If you want the newest iPhones then the best deals don’t tend to come before the spring and summer months. If you are happy to buy an older iPhone then you will probably see decent deals around Prime Day and Black Friday – but deals happen all year round.

We hope this article has proved helpful in reaching an informed buying decision. Remember that good prices can be found all year round, if a retailer is feeling generous and you know where to look: read our guide to the [best iPhone deals](https://www.macworld.com/article/672801/best-iphone-deals.html) for more on that.

Wondering how long Apple supports iPhones for? Read [How long do iPhones last.](https://www.macworld.com/article/675021/how-long-does-apple-support-iphones.html "How long do iPhones last")

entries.title: Your old iPhone is actually going to get faster next week
entries.content:
[Macworld](https://www.macworld.com)

When Apple releases [iOS 27](https://www.macworld.com/article/2986799/ios-27-new-iphone-features-release-date-beta-compatiblity-apple-intelligence-siri.html) Monday, the main highlight will be artificial intelligence, which is only available on newer phones (iPhone 15 Pro, and iPhone 16 and later). Head over to the iOS 27 site on Apple.com, and you’ll see a lot about the [new Siri AI](https://www.macworld.com/article/3164693/siri-ai-is-both-impressive-and-disappointing.html), [Apple Intelligence](https://www.macworld.com/article/3163291/i-hate-ai-but-even-i-cant-wait-to-try-these-10-features-on-my-iphone.html), and other features that [require the latest hardware](https://www.macworld.com/article/3159693/apple-just-killed-my-apple-intelligence-dreams.html) to run. Unsurprisingly, this might leave owners of older iPhones wondering what exactly they’ll gain from the update.

After spending some time testing the [iOS 27 beta](https://www.macworld.com/article/3172166/apple-releases-the-second-ios-27-developer-beta-for-testers.html) on an iPhone 11 Pro Max (the oldest iPhone supported by the update), I can report that iOS 27 is just as important for older iPhones—maybe even more so. Although they’ll miss out on the latest AI features, iOS 27 may be the best update older iPhones have received in years.

## iOS 27 makes older iPhones fast again

If you’ve installed iOS 26 on an older iPhone, you’ve probably noticed that some things weren’t exactly smooth. Even some of the latest iPhones had some trouble running the fancy animations added with Liquid Glass.

Earlier this year, I wrote about how [iOS 26 seemed noticeably buggy](https://www.macworld.com/article/3129163/ios-26-iphone-performance-battery-ios-27-wwdc.html) compared to other recent iOS releases. Animations stuttered more often, apps took longer to launch, and even basic system interactions sometimes felt sluggish.

Apple promised that iOS 27 would address many of these issues. Even before the [release candidate arrived](https://www.macworld.com/article/3172166/ios-27-beta-updates-features-release-date.html) this week, my tests with the [iPhone 11 Pro Max](https://www.macworld.com/article/233254) show that the company was serious about improving performance, especially when it comes to old hardware.

![Liquid Glass setting in iOS 27 on an iPhone 11 Pro Max](https://b2c-contenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Liquid-Glass-iOS-27.jpg?quality=50&strip=all&w=1200)

iOS 27 will bring some design refinements to Liquid Glass, but the real improvements are with performance.

Foundry

To get a better idea of how much has changed, I measured the time it takes to complete a handful of common tasks on the same iPhone 11 Pro Max running iOS 26 and iOS 27 beta 1.

I started with something simple that most people do every day: taking photos with their iPhone. On iOS 26, my iPhone 11 took 0.98 seconds to open the Camera app, then 3.61 seconds to take a photo and load it into my photo library.

I ran the test again with iOS 27, and the improvements were noticeable. Now it only takes about 0.65 seconds to open the Camera app, and 2.44 seconds to take a photo and immediately open it from the thumbnail preview. For users, this means a lower chance of missing an important shot because their phone is too slow.

Many iPhone users also rely on the Maps app every day, and on iOS 26, the iPhone 11 took a long 3.01 seconds to load it. With the first beta of iOS 27, the same iPhone now loads the Maps app in just 1.36 seconds. That’s twice as fast as on iOS 26.

Other actions, such as launching Safari, browsing the App Store, and opening the share sheet, are also noticeably faster in iOS 27.

### iOS 27 beta vs. iOS 26 speed tests

Results are in seconds. Lower results/shorter bars are better.

On their own, these numbers won’t transform the experience. After all, we’re talking about fractions of a second in some cases. But when you’re running these tasks multiple times a day, every second adds up to minutes saved. And the whole system feels remarkably faster.

## The smoother animations matter even more

Performance benchmarks are only part of the story. What really makes iOS 27 better on the iPhone 11 is how much smoother the animations feel during everyday use.

Visuals everywhere appear more consistent and less prone to frame drops. Swiping to open Control Center is noticeably more fluid. Unlocking the phone feels more responsive. App transitions seem better optimized and less likely to hitch.

Those were all things that bothered me when I tried using this iPhone on iOS 26, and now Apple seems to have fixed nearly all of the slow animations.

Once again, these aren’t dramatic changes individually, but together they create the impression that the old hardware is no longer struggling to keep up with the operating system. The result is an iPhone that feels newer than it actually is.

![holding an iPhone 17 pro Max (left) and iPhone 11 Pro Max showing their rear cameras](https://b2c-contenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/iPhone-17-and-iPhone-11.jpg?quality=50&strip=all&w=1200)

You won’t get all of the features that you get on the iPhone 17 PRI Max, but iOS 27 will still be an impressive upgrade for older iPhones.

Foundry

## iOS 27 also runs cooler

Another change I noticed almost immediately is the temperature. While my iPhone 11 Pro Max heats up quite easily on iOS 26, even when performing basic tasks, iOS 27 seems to keep the phone cool for longer. And that’s a great sign that the optimizations Apple made across the system have worked.

A cooler phone generally indicates that software processes are being managed more efficiently. It often means less unnecessary CPU and GPU activity, which can also translate into better battery life over time.

What’s more, these numbers were from one of the earlier betas, so it’s likely that the version Apple ships Monday will be even better for battery life.

## Older iPhones are getting a lot

If you watched the WWDC keynote, you might have been disappointed, as it seemed as though older iPhones wouldn’t be getting anything more than bug fixes with iOS 27. But that’s not actually the case. In fact, while devices like the iPhone 11 won’t support Siri AI, there are still many other new features coming to these devices.

One of my favorite new features in iOS 27 is the new clipboard shortcut right on the keyboard, which makes it faster to [paste text or even a screenshot](https://www.macworld.com/article/3162167/my-favorite-android-feature-just-landed-on-my-iphone-and-im-in-love.html) you just took. Being able to control the volume of the alarms and timers independently was also a nice addition.

![Paste feature in iOS 27 on an iPhone 11 Pro Max](https://b2c-contenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/iOS-27-keyboard.jpg?quality=50&strip=all&w=1200)

Older iPhones won’t miss out on small iOS 27 features like this clipboard upgrade in the keyboard.

Foundry

There’s also the ability to create custom passes in the Wallet app, a redesigned interface that makes it easier to play audio messages in iMessage, an option to save a high-resolution frame from a video in the Photos app, and larger Home Screen widgets.

All of these features are coming to older iPhones with iOS 27. Sure, they might not sound as exciting as a new AI assistant that can control your phone, but they’re exactly the kind of improvements that make your phone feel more useful and polished.

Not to mention that all iPhones getting iOS 27 will feature refinements to the Liquid Glass interface, including the new transparency slider that lets you choose the look you want.

## iOS 27 is a surprisingly great update for aging iPhones

To be honest, I was quite surprised when Apple confirmed that even the iPhone 11 would get the iOS 27 update. After all, my experience running iOS 26 on that generation of phone was quite frustrating. But now that I’ve tried the first beta, I can see why Apple made that decision.

The main narrative surrounding iOS 27 focuses heavily on AI, and that’s completely understandable. Apple had been lagging behind in this race, so it’s no surprise that they want to make a big deal out of all the new Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features.

![typing on an iPhone 11 Pro Max](https://b2c-contenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/iPhone-11-Pro-Max.jpg?quality=50&strip=all&w=1200)

Don’t worry about missing out on Siri AI. iOS 27 is a fantastic upgrade for older iPhones.

Foundry

Yet, after using iOS 27 on an iPhone 11 Pro Max, I can’t help but think that older devices may be among the biggest beneficiaries of this update. The software feels faster. Animations are smoother. The phone runs cooler. And users still get a collection of useful new features despite missing out on AI.

For anyone worried that iOS 27 would leave older iPhones behind, the first beta suggests the opposite. Apple appears to have spent just as much time optimizing the experience for existing users as it did building features for future hardware, and that’s great news for people still holding onto a seven-year-old iPhone.

entries.title: Introducing automatic remediation policies with Cloudflare CASB
entries.content:
Today, we’re making Cloudflare CASB more powerful than ever by introducing automatic remediation policies. This means security teams can now design event-driven logic to revoke risky file shares and dispatch custom webhooks, without manual intervention.

When we launched [Cloudflare CASB](https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-zero-trust-casb/), a cloud access security broker, we wanted to provide security teams complete visibility into the posture of their SaaS applications before misconfigurations became incidents. With a quick, clientless integration, CASB surfaces risks like overshared files, dormant admin keys and tokens, OAuth apps with excessive permissions — continuously, across users in the organization.

For years, [SaaS Security Posture Management](https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/cloud/what-is-sspm/) (SSPM) tools such as Cloudflare CASB have functioned as a passive alarm system. Most SSPM tools tell you what’s wrong but do not help you fix the issue, placing the burden on administrators to manage an ever-growing to-do list. A single misconfigured file-sharing policy across a Google Workspace tenant can generate thousands of findings in seconds, and even a disciplined team faces a window between detection and remediation measured in hours or days — more than enough time for a sensitive file to be downloaded, forwarded, or indexed.

With automatic remediation policies, CASB customers can now configure the actions that should be invoked immediately after a new finding is identified.

## Shifting from reactive to proactive

When we launched [manual remediation actions](https://blog.cloudflare.com/remediation-in-cloudflare-casb/) earlier this year, we gave security teams the ability to resolve misconfigurations directly from the Cloudflare dashboard. This removed the need for customers to log in to multiple SaaS portals to take action on the security and content findings detected by Cloudflare CASB. Still, this required a human to confirm and initiate each individual remediation — even if they’d seen this exact finding type before.

CASB policies are a native automation engine built directly into [Cloudflare One](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/) that takes action the moment a finding is detected. Security teams define their response logic once, whether that is revoking access to a file share, dispatching a webhook to your security operations center (SOC), or forwarding the event to a security orchestration, automation and response platform (SOAR). The engine handles matches automatically by executing the customer-configured action.

As an example, many organizations implement controls that prohibit files from being shared publicly. However, they may apply an exception to users and groups in their marketing department who are frequently required to collaborate with external parties. SSPMs allow their customers to be alerted of any files that are shared publicly in violation of their policy. With many solutions, this permitted behavior lands in a queue with hundreds of possible violations, forcing administrators to take action on each individual instance.

CASB policies are designed for exactly this scenario. Rather than waiting for a human to see and act on a finding, automation fires the moment detection happens. The public share is revoked within minutes, keeping the backlog of findings clean and clear.

## How CASB policies work

At their core, CASB policies are automated workflows that tell our scanning service what action to take when a new finding is detected. From there, the configured policy will tell CASB to either trigger a remediation action, send a webhook, or both. This gives organizations the flexibility to rely on native CASB remediation capabilities or their own internal automation services and communication channels — without having to take action in disparate platforms or create their own event processing system.

## How we built it

The architecture behind CASB policies is built entirely on the Cloudflare developer platform — the same platform available to every Cloudflare customer.

When a finding is detected, the findings engine enqueues an orchestration message to a [Cloudflare Queue](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/). A [Worker](https://workers.cloudflare.com/) consumer then checks whether a policy configuration matches the incoming finding. If a match exists, it creates the corresponding job and hands it to the remediations pipeline, which runs on [Cloudflare Workflows](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/) for durable, fault-tolerant execution. That means jobs survive process restarts and retries are handled automatically.

Cloudflare Workflows also handle third-party API rate limits gracefully. If a vendor returns a rate limit error, the Workflow pauses for the appropriate backoff window and retries without dropping the job. Our target from detection to completed remediation is five minutes or less.

## How to create policies

To get started, navigate to the Cloudflare dashboard and create your first policy. Policies can include both a remediation and a webhook action, but at a minimum:

* **Select the vendor.** Select the vendor and integration or tenant this policy should apply to.
* **Select the integration.** You can hand-select specific integrations or set it to apply to all integrations for the selected vendor.
* **Choose a finding type.** Select the CASB finding type that should fire the policy.
* **Choose an action.** Once a trigger is selected, the available actions for that finding type are shown. There are two categories:
  + **Run remediations.** First-party actions Cloudflare performs directly against the SaaS integration API. CASB currently supports remediation actions for Microsoft and Google Workspace file/folder finding types. Note that this may require [upgrading permissions](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/cloud-and-saas-findings/manage-findings/#configure-remediation-permissions) on integrations to read/write.
  + **Send webhooks.** Send finding details to configured [webhook destinations](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/integrations/cloud-and-saas/webhooks/) such as Slack, Microsoft Teams, Jira, ServiceNow, Tines, or any custom HTTP endpoint your team uses.

### Example webhook format

## Maintaining visibility and compliance

Each policy action produces two categories of logs, visible under Insights in Cloudflare One.

**Admin Activity logs.** These capture changes to a policy definition: who created it, who edited it, who disabled it, and when. If a policy was turned off and a risk slipped through, this audit trail surfaces a timeline of the event.

**Cloud & SaaS Security policies logs.** This new class of logs captures the runtime outcome of policy invocations. This includes details like which finding triggered the policy, which file was acted on, whether it succeeded or failed, and the specific error if it did not — for example, a 401 Unauthorized or an API rate limit response from the vendor.

For compliance use cases, the execution log is the proof of fix. It ties a specific finding, like an overshared file (e.g. Q4\_Financials.pdf), to a specific automated action and event timestamp.

## Get started

Customers can find CASB Policies in the **Cloud & SaaS findings** section of the dashboard today. Connect or update your Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace integration to Read-Write permissions, and create your first remediation policy.

In the coming weeks, we’ll also be adding support for Custom Findings to CASB. Different organizations have unique needs when it comes to detection, and we want to give customers the ability to augment or define finding logic to fit those needs.

New to Cloudflare One? [Sign up for 50 free seats](https://dash.cloudflare.com/sign-up/zero-trust) to get started with CASB, or [talk to our team](https://www.cloudflare.com/contact/sase/) about a deployment at scale. For full setup instructions, visit our [developer documentation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/).
